# Joinery and Fasteners

CAD makes every joint look perfect. Wood does not. This chapter is about
modeling joints at the level of fit: enough detail to check the geometry, not
so much that the model becomes a furniture-rendering exercise.

## What you will learn

- How to represent common carpentry joints.
- How to size clearance holes and pockets.
- When a fastener should be geometry and when it should be a note.
- How to check a joint for overlap and clearance.

## Model the fit, not the craft

A joint has three jobs in a model:

1. Reserve the material that must be removed.
2. Show the assembled relationship between the parts.
3. Give you a dimension you can transfer to the shop.

It does not need to show every saw mark, glue line, or grain direction. A clean
notch with the right dimensions is more useful than a sculpted mortise with
rounded internal corners that no chisel will produce.

## Common joints and how to model them

| Joint | Modeling approach | What to check |
|-------|-------------------|---------------|
| Butt joint | Two bodies meet at a face | Faces are coplanar; fastener clearance |
| Half-lap | Cut half the depth from each member | Lap depth; flush outer faces |
| Notch | Cut a pocket in one member | Pocket width/length; clearance |
| Mortise and tenon | Pocket in one member, projecting tenon on the other | Tenon thickness; mortise clearance; haunch |
| Dado / groove | Cut a channel across a board | Channel width; board thickness |
| Bolt connection | Clearance hole through both members | Hole diameter; washer face; edge distance |

For a glued joint, model the nominal dimensions. For a joint that must come
apart, or that will be assembled on a sloped site, add a small clearance. A
1 mm clearance is a useful default for a part that should slide; use the
fastener manufacturer's hole size for bolts.

## Fasteners: geometry or note?

Model a fastener as geometry when:

- it passes through a visible face;
- its head or washer needs a bearing surface;
- it determines an edge distance or a collision;
- a client needs to see how the connection works.

Keep it as a note or a BOM line when:

- it is a hidden screw or nail;
- the exact length depends on site conditions;
- modeling it would add detail without changing a decision.

Do not model threads for a through-bolt. A clearance cylinder is enough. Do not
model every screw in a deck; a note such as "two 65 mm screws per board at each
joist" belongs in the build notes.

## Edge distance and clearance

A bolt too close to the edge of a board will split it. The model can show the
distance even if the structural rule comes from code or the manufacturer.

Check:

- distance from the hole centre to the edge;
- washer diameter versus face width;
- clearance for a wrench or socket;
- whether two fasteners collide inside the joint;
- whether a bolt head protrudes into a moving part.

## Build along: a half-lap gate frame

1. Build two 90 × 90 mm gate stiles, 1800 mm long.
2. Build two 90 × 90 mm rails, sized to fit between the stiles.
3. At each crossing, cut half the depth from the stile and half from the rail.
4. Assemble the four parts and check that the outer faces are flush.
5. Add a diagonal brace and check that it does not protrude through the faces.
6. Check clearance between the gate and its posts.

## Checks

- No unintended overlap between bodies.
- Lap depth is half the member thickness, unless the design says otherwise.
- Outer faces are flush after assembly.
- Bolt holes line up through both members.
- The gate has clearance to swing through its full arc.
- The diagonal brace does not create a zero-thickness intersection.

## Exercises

1. Notch a 90 × 90 post for a 45 × 140 rail with 1 mm clearance.
2. Model a mortise-and-tenon joint at 1:3 thickness ratio. Check the mortise
   walls are not paper-thin.
3. Add an M10 clearance hole through a 90 mm post. What hole diameter did you
   use, and why?
4. Model a lag-screw connection as a pilot hole plus a washer face. Decide what
   belongs in the BOM instead of the geometry.
